## Overview

The Tagbanwa are an indigenous people of the Philippines and one of the country’s oldest ethnic groups. They are mainly found in central and northern Palawan. Central Tagbanwas live along the western and eastern coastal areas of central Palawan, especially in Aborlan, Quezon, and Puerto Princesa. Calamian Tagbanwa communities are found on the Baras coast, Busuanga Island, Coron Island, and in parts of El Nido. The two major subgroups speak related languages with differences in tone and pronunciation and do not have exactly the same customs. The Tagbanwa are associated with fishing, farming, gathering, weaving, pottery, basketry, woodcarving, ritual, and a close relationship with the natural world. They have also maintained ancestral-domain claims and traditions despite land grabbing, modernization, migration, and religious change.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources describe Tagbanwa bark clothing and basketry.

**Tingkop** — The *tingkop* is a harvest basket made from blackened and natural bamboo. Tagbanwa makers apply numerous designs so that the natural and darkened materials create contrasting patterns.

**Cone-shaped basket** — This basket uses black and natural bamboo designs on the outside. The center is made from a bamboo strip skived slightly smaller to create even holes, while close weaving toward the top produces a funnel effect.

**Bayong-bayong** — The soft rice basket called *bayong-bayong* has a square base and a round top. Plain buri sides are overlaid with colored buri to form block and V-shapes, and dyed palm leaves add color to the weaving.

**Bark cloth** — Traditional clothing was made from the inner bark of the salugin tree. The bark was beaten with a mallet until it became soft, then washed and dried in the sun.

**Motif vocabulary.** Block shapes, V-shapes, black-and-natural bamboo contrast, designs formed by dyed palm leaves.

### Clothing & dress

Traditional Tagbanwa clothing was made from the bark of trees, particularly salugin. Men formerly wore simple loincloths held by a woven rattan waistband called *ambalad*, while women wore brief wraparound skirts made from bark. The Tagbanua later adopted some articles of Muslim clothing, and western-type clothing is now also worn. Tagbanwa women wear bright body ornament and brightly colored clothes. They dress like non-tribe lowlanders, while some elder men prefer G-strings for comfort when tilling fields or fishing.

### Architecture

Tagbanwa houses are made with bamboo and wood forming a strong frame, anahaw leaves serving as roof and walls, and bamboo slats used for flooring. Tagbanwa live in compact villages containing between 45 and 500 individuals. Ritual life also requires special structures, including ceremonial platforms and rafts. During the *runsay*, a ceremonial raft called the *bangkaran* or *banglay* is built for offerings and is sent seaward.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The Tagbanwa are skilled in pottery. Earlier records describe their use of brass rings and chains, bells, knives, and copper wire for binding fish hooks. Wooden combs, bracelets, baskets, ritual bowls, and carved animal figures are also documented. The most notable present-day artistic products are baskets and woodcarvings. Blackened carvings expose the original white grain of the wood through simple etched or incised features. Named carved forms include *mammanuk*, a rooster; *kiruman*, a turtle; *kararaga*, a native bird; and *dugyan*, a small ground animal.

### Jewelry & body adornment

In the past, Tagbanwa men and women wore their hair long, filed and blackened their teeth, and used earplugs carved from the hardwood bantilinaw. Women wore bead necklaces that covered the neck, as well as anklets made from copper and brass wire. Tagbanwa women are described as wearing bright body ornament. Wooden bracelets and carved wooden combs were also made.

## Music & performance

Tagbanwa ritual and social gatherings formerly included an assortment of musical instruments. These included the *aruding*, or jaw harp; the *babarak*, or nose flute; and the *tipanu*, or mouth flute. The *pagang* and *tibuldu* were two forms of bamboo tube zither. The *kudlung* was a boat lute, while the *gimbal* was a drum whose top was made from the skin of the *bayawak*, or monitor lizard. The *tiring* consisted of bamboo lengths with openings of different sizes that produced different notes when struck with a stick. Two generic types of gongs were obtained from the shallow *babandil*.

The mouth flute remains in use, while gongs and drums are still played during rituals. Modern acoustic guitar and ukulele, the latter fashioned from half a coconut shell, have replaced some of the other instruments. Music accompanies ritual, dancing, ceremonial feasts, and social gatherings. In the *andardi*, a festival dance performed in and around Aborlan, the music consists of one part of twelve measures played or sung continuously. Drums or gongs accompany the music and song.

## Dance & theatre

The sources name numerous Tagbanwa dances connected with ritual, festivals, healing, courtship, work, and social gatherings. *Abellano*, also called *soriano*, is a traditional dance performed by males. *Bugas-bugasan* is performed by all participants in a *pagdiwata* after they drink ceremonial *tabad*, or rice wine. *Kalindapan* is a solo dance by the female *babaylan* and her attendants. *Runsay* consists of ritual dances performed by villagers on the seashore while a bamboo raft carrying food offerings is floated for the gods.

*Sarungkay* is a healing dance in which the main *babaylan* balances a sword on her head and waves *ugsang*, or strips of palm leaf. *Tugatak* and *tarindak* are performed by villagers attending an *inim* or *pagdiwata*. *Tamigan* is performed by male combatants using round winnowers called *bilao* as shields.

At the *albarka* ritual, guests watch *busak-busak*, the spider dance; *batak ribid*, which simulates gathering *camote*; *bungalon*, a showing-off dance; *bugsay-bugsay*, a paddle dance using fans; *segutset*, a courtship dance; and *tarek*, a traditional dance. Drama is expressed through mimetic dances imitating animals or occupations, while ritual possession involves the priestess taking the role of the deity receiving offerings.

## Festivals & rituals

Tagbanwa ritual life is based on interaction between the living, the dead, spirits, and the natural environment. Ceremonial feasts and rituals may be held within the family or led by a community leader. Offerings include rice, chicken, and betel nut. A large feast is celebrated after each harvest to honor the deities, with singing, dancing, courting, and blood compacts.

The *lambay* is held twice each year. The first is in January, when the people appeal for sunshine and winds to dry the forests for clearing and planting. The second is in May, when they ask for moderate rains to help upland rice grow. The *pagbuyis* is performed three times a year: first in November, second in December, and third when the moon can be seen during the daytime, a time called *magkaaldawan*.

The *runsay* is observed once a year at night, on the fourth day after the full moon of December, on the beach near the mouth of the Aborlan River. It begins at dusk and ends at dawn and seeks protection against epidemic. Its five phases include building the *bangkaran* or *banglay*, invoking spirits and deities, offering food, tying a chicken to the platform, sending the raft toward the sea, and singing and dancing after it disappears.

The *bilang* is a major ritual for the dead and takes place after the rice harvest, when *tabad* is plentiful. It includes divination, offerings near the grave, invocation of spirit relatives, incense, gongs, communal food, and drinking *tabad* through reed straws. When a person dies, the soul remains on earth for seven days until the *kapupusan*, or rites for the dead, are completed.

## Foodways

The sources identify rice as a central food and agricultural crop. Tagbanwa cultivate rice in swidden, or *kaingin*, fields intercropped with sweet potato, corn, and cassava. Coastal communities fish and exchange fish for agricultural products. Forest products, including gum, rattan, and honey, are also gathered.

Rice wine called *tabad* is important in ritual and social life. Participants in *bugas-bugasan* drink ceremonial *tabad*, and communal drinking through reed straws follows the *bilang* ceremony. In the annual feast for the deities, chickens and roosters are brought for the ceremony; the fowl that die are seasoned, cooked, and eaten. Offerings in other rituals include rice, chicken, betel nut, and food placed on ceremonial rafts.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources record Tagbanwa folk history, mythology, religious explanations, and ritual invocations. Folk history describes an early relationship with Brunei and the first sultan of Brunyu, from a place called Burnay. Antonio Pigafetta recorded Tagbanwa practices in 1521, including blood compact, cultivation, hunting with blowpipes and wooden arrows, and the distillation of rice wine.

Tagbanwa mythology describes the spirit world, the gods, the fate of souls, and ritual obligations. The four major deities are Mangindusa or Nagabacaban, Polo, Sedumunadoc, and Tabiacoud. Other beings include the diwatas, Bugawasin, Tungkuyanin, Tumangkuyun, Bulalakaw, Taliyakad, and Anggugru.

## Language & religion

The Tagbanwa have native languages called Aborlan Tagbanwa, Calamian Tagbanwa, and Central Tagbanwa, as well as their own writing system. They are also proficient in Palawano and may speak or understand Tandulanon, Silanganon, Baras, Tagalog, Batak, Cuyonon, and Calawian in varying ways.

Tagbanwa religious belief includes heaven, hell, the human soul, spirits inhabiting the natural world, and rituals intended to appease or gain the favor of those spirits. The *babaylan* performs rituals from birth to death, provides charms for hunters and fishers, and cures ailments. The Tagbanwa are believed to have six souls: one true soul called *kiyarulwa* and five secondary souls called the *payu*. Northern Tagbanwa on Coron Island are now predominantly Christians because of evangelization by foreign missionaries during the late sixties and seventies.
